calls.reason: The packet has no agreed test of whether a system has a 'proper model' and no study linking that to reasoning about time or prices, so this necessity claim can't be called.

Karvonen's chess study finds board-state representations that respond to interventions, which challenges the premise. But it covers one specialist model, and nothing tests the claimed cause across general LLMs.
There is no inspectable record of the original GPT-5 task and no task-specific causal analysis. Gurnee and Tegmark's study is about other models, so the cause of the errors is unknown.
No source tests the same system for both a robust chess-rules model and 'all it needs to know' about time and finance. Both terms are undefined, so the conditional can't be checked.

Tom's Guide (Aug 12, 2025) reports that no model, GPT-5 included, beat the 83.7% human baseline on SimpleBench's commonsense questions. That points to recurring failures, though how often they occur in everyday use is unmeasured.

RuleArena shows failures when rules are supplied in the prompt, while a fine-tuned small model almost always made legal chess moves. Neither shows that a missing abstract model is the cause, so the evidence is mixed.
